strengths: The authors propose a continuous optimization model that is different from existing methods and could be applied to various low-rank representations such as CP, Tucker, and TT formats.
The proposed method demonstrates significant improvements in both accuracy and efficiency over existing works in numerical experiments, suggesting practical usefulness.
The results regarding convergence of the method would make the approach valuable for a reasonably formulated problem.

The paper presents an algorithm that significantly improves upon existing methods by achieving remarkable advances in both accuracy and efficiency, with superior performance compared to existing methods and applicability to various low-rank representations including CP, Tucker, and TT formats.
The authors employ precise mathematical notations consistently, facilitating understanding of the proposed algorithm, theoretical analysis, and numerical experiments.
The paper is generally well structured and written.
In some cases good results are obtained when searching for CP-tensors minimum.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 formulates an equivalent optimization problem for finding the largest element in a tensor, but the paper does not provide an in-depth analysis of this equivalent problem, lacking discussion of the number of minimizers, convexity/concavity, and other properties of the objective function.

Theorem 2 only shows convergence of a subsequence to a stationary point, without guaranteeing that the entire sequence converges or that it converges to the optimal solution, and it does not address possible limit cycles or other non-convergent behaviors of the alternating iterative algorithm.

Theorem 3 establishes a linear convergence rate under the assumption that the initial point is sufficiently close to the optimal solution, but the paper provides no guidance on obtaining such an initial point and does not explore the existence of multiple optimal solutions that could affect convergence.
The symmetric tensor eigenvalue formulation is mentioned in Section II but symmetry is never enforced thereafter, despite rank‑1 factor components typically being identical in the symmetric case.

The proof of Theorem 1 appears incomplete or incorrect; convergence is argued only based on the objective function, which is insufficient and does not properly contrast with convergence of standard alternating least squares.
The paper takes known algorithms and only connects them together in the special case of finding the extremum of CP‑tensors.
Comparisons in numerical examples are given with only two (or one) other methods, which is clearly insufficient to substantiate the claims.
The coloring in the tables highlights only the presented method when both methods are best, instead of coloring all cases where a particular method is the best.
Table 1 comparisons are not entirely honest; the star‑sampling method can be adapted to find minima via a simple transformation, making the claimed contribution of the new approach negligible.

For the Rastrigin and Schwefel model functions, using CP‑compression with the new method yields results that are essentially identical to those of the existing optima_tt algorithm, rendering the contribution meaningless.
No code is provided so that experiments can be repeated.
The theorems in the paper are rather trivial, and one of them is not proved at all, resulting in a lack of serious convergence analysis.
In the proof of Theorem 1 the notation "x^{(n)}=1" is unclear; the equivalence to problem (2.3) is questionable, and the theorem is never proved in the paper.

Times reported in Table 4 for experiments with real‑world data are not relevant because they omit the cost of compressing the data into CP format, and the reported runtimes would be much faster if the full tensor were expanded.
The paper claims the algorithm is parameter‑free, yet the final algorithm includes an adjustable parameter b.
